title: Electricity and Electromagnetism
tagline: Understand electric circuits, power, household electricity and magnetic effects of current.

overview.intro: Electricity and electromagnetism connect electric current, circuits, energy consumption and magnetic effects. This chapter covers current, potential difference, resistance, Ohm’s law, series and parallel circuits, electrical power and energy, household wiring and safety, and the magnetic effect of current including electromagnets and electromagnetic induction at an introductory level. Accurate circuit reasoning, units and safe-use principles are central.

facts.label: Ohm’s law
facts.value: V = IR (at constant temperature for ohmic conductors)

learningOutcomes: Define electric current, potential difference, resistance and state Ohm’s law.
Analyse simple series and parallel circuits and calculate equivalent resistance.
Calculate electrical power and energy consumption and interpret household units.
Explain household wiring, fuses/MCBs, earthing and safe practices.
Describe magnetic effects of current, electromagnets and basic electromagnetic induction.

blocks.text: Electric current is the rate of flow of electric charge through a conductor, measured in amperes (A). Potential difference between two points is the work done per unit charge in moving charge between them, measured in volts (V). Resistance is the opposition offered by a conductor to current, measured in ohms (Ω).

Ohm’s law states that the current through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it, provided physical conditions such as temperature remain constant: V = IR. Conductors obeying Ohm’s law have a linear V–I relationship. Resistance depends on length, cross-sectional area, material and temperature.

items.text: If V = 6 V and R = 3 Ω, then I = V/R = 2 A.
items.note: Apply Ohm’s law with consistent units.

items.text: A longer or thinner wire has greater resistance than a shorter or thicker wire of same material.

blocks.text: In a series circuit, components are connected end-to-end so the same current flows through each component, while the total potential difference is the sum of potential differences across components. Equivalent resistance is R_eq = R1 + R2 + ... . If one component fails in a simple series path, current stops flowing.

In a parallel circuit, components are connected across the same two points so the potential difference across each branch is the same, while total current is the sum of branch currents. Equivalent resistance is given by 1/R_eq = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + ... and is less than the smallest branch resistance. Household appliances are connected in parallel for independent operation.

learn.title: Electrical Power, Energy and Household Electricity

blocks.text: Electrical power is the rate at which electrical energy is consumed or converted, given by P = VI. Using Ohm’s law, P = I^2R = V^2/R. Electrical energy consumed over time t is E = Pt. In homes, energy is measured in kilowatt-hours (kWh), where 1 kWh is the energy used by a 1 kW appliance in 1 hour.

Household circuits typically use a live wire and neutral wire, with an earth wire for safety in appliances with metal bodies. Fuses and miniature circuit breakers (MCBs) protect circuits from excessive current due to overload or short circuit. Earthing provides a low-resistance path to ground, reducing risk of electric shock.

items: Parallel wiring allows appliances to operate independently at rated voltage.
A fuse melts and breaks the circuit when current exceeds its rating.
Earthing protects users from leakage current in faulty appliances.
Switches are connected in the live wire for safe isolation.

learn.title: Magnetic Effect of Current and Electromagnets

blocks.text: A current-carrying conductor produces a magnetic field around it. The direction of the magnetic field around a straight conductor can be found using the right-hand thumb rule. A current-carrying solenoid produces a magnetic field similar to a bar magnet, with distinct north and south poles.

An electromagnet is made by winding insulated wire around a soft iron core and passing current through it. Its strength depends on current, number of turns and core material, and it can be switched on or off. Electromagnets are used in electric bells, relays, cranes and many devices, unlike permanent magnets which retain magnetism.

items.meaning: A temporary magnet produced when current flows through a coil around a soft iron core.
A coil of wire that produces a magnetic field when current passes through it.
Rule to determine magnetic field direction around a current-carrying conductor.

blocks.text: Electromagnetic induction is the phenomenon of producing an induced current or electromotive force in a conductor when the magnetic field linked with it changes. This can occur by moving a magnet near a coil, moving a coil in a magnetic field, or changing current in a nearby circuit. The magnitude of induced current depends on the rate of change of magnetic flux and other factors.

Electromagnetic induction is the principle behind electric generators and transformers. In practical applications, alternating current (AC) is commonly used for transmission because its voltage can be stepped up or down efficiently. Understanding basic induction helps connect magnetism and electricity as interrelated effects.

items: Changing magnetic field linkage induces current in a closed circuit.
Generators convert mechanical energy to electrical energy by induction.
Transformers work on electromagnetic induction with alternating current.
Electrical safety and correct circuit design are essential in applications.

keyPoints: Ohm’s law: V = IR under constant physical conditions.
Series circuits have same current; parallel circuits have same potential difference.
Equivalent resistance increases in series and decreases in parallel combinations.
Electrical power P = VI and energy E = Pt; 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10^6 J.
Household appliances are wired in parallel and protected by fuses/MCBs and earthing.
Current-carrying conductors produce magnetic fields; solenoids act like bar magnets.
Electromagnets are temporary magnets whose strength depends on current and turns.
Electromagnetic induction produces induced current when magnetic flux changes.
Correct units (A, V, Ω, W, kWh) and circuit connections are essential.
Safety practices reduce risks of shock, overload and short circuits.

questions.prompt: Ohm’s law is expressed as:
questions.answer: V = IR
questions.explanation: Potential difference equals current multiplied by resistance for an ohmic conductor.
questions.commonMistake: Rearrange correctly when solving for I or R.

questions.prompt: The SI unit of electric power is:
questions.answer: watt
questions.explanation: Power is the rate of energy transfer and is measured in watts.
questions.commonMistake: Joule is the unit of energy, not power.

questions.prompt: Two resistors of 2 Ω and 4 Ω are connected in series. Their equivalent resistance is:
questions.answer: 6 Ω
questions.explanation: In series, equivalent resistance is the sum: 2 + 4 = 6 Ω.
questions.commonMistake: Use reciprocal formula only for parallel combinations.

questions.prompt: Household electrical appliances are connected in parallel because:
options: each gets full voltage and works independently
questions.answer: each gets full voltage and works independently
questions.explanation: Parallel connection provides the same potential difference across each appliance and allows independent operation.
questions.commonMistake: In series, failure of one appliance can break the circuit.

questions.prompt: A fuse is connected in the:
questions.answer: live wire
questions.explanation: Placing the fuse in the live wire ensures the circuit is disconnected from supply when current is excessive.
questions.commonMistake: A fuse in the neutral wire may not isolate the appliance from live potential.

questions.prompt: The commercial unit of electrical energy is:
questions.answer: kilowatt-hour
questions.explanation: Electricity consumption is billed in kilowatt-hours (kWh).
questions.commonMistake: Kilowatt is a unit of power, not energy.

questions.prompt: An electromagnet is made using a core of:
questions.answer: soft iron
questions.explanation: Soft iron is used because it magnetises strongly when current flows and loses magnetism when current stops.
questions.commonMistake: Steel retains magnetism and is used for permanent magnets.

questions.prompt: Two resistors of 6 Ω each are connected in parallel. The equivalent resistance is:
questions.answer: 3 Ω
questions.explanation: For equal resistors in parallel, R_eq = R/n = 6/2 = 3 Ω.
questions.commonMistake: Parallel equivalent resistance is always less than the smallest branch resistance.

questions.prompt: The opposition offered to the flow of current in a conductor is called ________.
questions.answer: resistance
questions.explanation: Resistance is measured in ohms (Ω).
questions.commonMistake: Do not confuse resistance with resistivity (material property).

questions.prompt: The safety wire connected to the metal body of an appliance is the ________ wire.
questions.answer: earth
questions.explanation: Earthing provides a path for leakage current to prevent electric shock.
questions.commonMistake: The live wire carries current from supply; the earth wire is for safety.

questions.prompt: Production of induced current due to change in magnetic field is called electromagnetic ________.
questions.answer: induction
questions.explanation: Electromagnetic induction is the basis of generators and transformers.
questions.commonMistake: Magnetic effect of current is the reverse phenomenon.

questions.prompt: State Ohm’s law.
questions.answer: Ohm’s law states that the current flowing through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across its ends, provided physical conditions such as temperature remain constant (V = IR).
questions.explanation: The condition of constant temperature is important for ohmic conductors.
questions.commonMistake: Include the proportionality condition, not just the formula.

questions.prompt: Calculate the current flowing through a 12 Ω resistor when a potential difference of 6 V is applied across it.
questions.answer: Using Ohm’s law, I = V/R = 6/12 = 0.5 A.
questions.explanation: Current is potential difference divided by resistance.
questions.commonMistake: Use consistent SI units and include the unit ampere.

questions.prompt: State two differences between series and parallel circuits.
questions.answer: In a series circuit the same current flows through all components, whereas in a parallel circuit the current divides among branches. In a series circuit the potential difference divides across components, whereas in a parallel circuit the same potential difference exists across each branch.
questions.explanation: Current and voltage distribution are the key differences.
questions.commonMistake: Give corresponding differences clearly for both circuit types.

questions.prompt: An electric bulb is rated 100 W, 220 V. Calculate the current drawn by it when operated at rated voltage.
questions.answer: Power P = VI, so current I = P/V = 100/220 = 0.4545 A (approximately 0.45 A).
questions.explanation: Use rated values to find operating current.
questions.commonMistake: Do not confuse power rating with energy consumed over time.

questions.prompt: Explain the functions of fuse and earthing in household electrical circuits.
questions.answer: A fuse is a safety device connected in the live wire that contains a thin wire of low melting point. If current exceeds the safe limit due to overload or short circuit, the fuse wire melts and breaks the circuit, preventing damage and fire. Earthing connects the metal body of an appliance to the ground through a low-resistance wire. If insulation fails and the live wire touches the metal body, current flows to earth instead of through a person touching the appliance, reducing the risk of electric shock and often causing the fuse/MCB to trip.
questions.explanation: Both devices protect users and equipment from electrical faults.
questions.commonMistake: State where each is connected and how it provides safety.

questions.prompt: Three resistors of 2 Ω, 3 Ω and 6 Ω are connected in parallel. Calculate the equivalent resistance of the combination.
questions.answer: For parallel combination, 1/R_eq = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3 = 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/6. Taking common denominator 6, 1/R_eq = (3 + 2 + 1)/6 = 6/6 = 1. Therefore, R_eq = 1 Ω.
questions.explanation: Add reciprocals of resistances and then take reciprocal of the sum.
questions.commonMistake: Do not add resistances directly for a parallel circuit.

questions.prompt: Describe the construction and working principle of an electromagnet. State two factors affecting its strength and two uses.
questions.answer: An electromagnet consists of a soft iron core wrapped with many turns of insulated copper wire (solenoid). When electric current passes through the coil, the core becomes magnetised and behaves like a magnet; when current is switched off, it loses most of its magnetism. Its strength increases with increase in current and number of turns, and also depends on the core material. Uses include electric bells, relays, cranes for lifting scrap iron and magnetic separation devices.
questions.explanation: Temporary magnetism and controllable strength make electromagnets useful in devices.
questions.commonMistake: Use soft iron core, not steel, for a strong temporary electromagnet.

questions.prompt: A household uses a 1 kW heater for 2 hours and four 100 W bulbs for 5 hours daily. Calculate the total electrical energy consumed in one day in kWh.
questions.answer: Energy consumed by heater = 1 kW × 2 h = 2 kWh. Power of four bulbs = 4 × 100 W = 400 W = 0.4 kW. Energy consumed by bulbs = 0.4 kW × 5 h = 2 kWh. Total energy consumed in one day = 2 + 2 = 4 kWh.
questions.explanation: Convert watts to kilowatts before multiplying by hours to get kWh.
questions.commonMistake: Account for all four bulbs and use consistent units.

questions.prompt: Why is a switch always connected in the live wire of a circuit rather than in the neutral wire?
questions.answer: The live wire is at supply potential, while the neutral wire is near earth potential. Connecting the switch in the live wire ensures that when the switch is off, the appliance is disconnected from the high potential supply and becomes safe to touch. If the switch were in the neutral wire, the appliance could remain connected to the live wire even when switched off, posing a risk of electric shock.
questions.explanation: Safety depends on isolating the appliance from live potential.
questions.commonMistake: Explain in terms of potential and shock risk, not just circuit completion.

questions.prompt: A 60 W bulb and a 100 W bulb are designed for the same voltage. Which has higher resistance and which draws more current when connected to that voltage? Justify using formulae.
questions.answer: For the same voltage V, power P = V^2/R, so resistance R = V^2/P. Since the 60 W bulb has lower power, R_60 = V^2/60 is greater than R_100 = V^2/100. Thus the 60 W bulb has higher resistance. Current I = P/V, so I_60 = 60/V and I_100 = 100/V. Therefore the 100 W bulb draws more current at the same voltage.
questions.explanation: At constant voltage, lower power implies higher resistance and lower current.
questions.commonMistake: Do not assume higher wattage means higher resistance; it is the opposite at same voltage.

questions.prompt: Explain how electromagnetic induction can be demonstrated using a coil and a bar magnet.
questions.answer: Connect a coil to a sensitive galvanometer. When a bar magnet is pushed towards the coil, the galvanometer shows a deflection indicating an induced current. When the magnet is pulled away, the deflection is in the opposite direction. If the magnet is stationary relative to the coil, there is no deflection. This shows that an induced current is produced only when there is a change in magnetic field linkage with the coil.
questions.explanation: Relative motion changes magnetic flux through the coil, inducing current.
questions.commonMistake: State observations for motion towards, away and at rest.
